fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A jar of colloidal silver started it all", "body": "Austin Walters traces his whole path back to about 2003, when he was flattened by the flu with no health insurance and a friend's mother sent over a mason jar of what looked like pee. It was colloidal silver, and he says the fever and aches were gone by the next day. That single turnaround convinced him something was being left out of the story he had been told about health. He taught himself electrolysis, bought fine silver from a jewelry store, wired alligator clips to a nine volt converter from Radio Shack, and brewed his own for years."}, {"title": "Why the blue man is the wrong lesson", "body": "The famous warning against colloidal silver is the blue man, whose skin turned a bluish gray from a condition called argyria. Austin explains that the man made his silver with ordinary tap water, so the silver particles bonded to chlorine and other minerals, grew too heavy, and lodged in fatty tissue. Made properly with distilled water, and skimming off the black silver oxide that forms on top, he says that outcome does not happen. Chance Garton notes how reliably the worst case scenario is the version that reaches the masses, while Austin adds that we fear what we do not understand."}, {"title": "How one NASA talk created biomagnetism", "body": "The origin story runs through Bob Beck, blood electrification and pulsed electromagnetic field devices, then lands on October 10th of 1988. Doctor Isaac Goiz Duran heard a NASA physician, Doctor Broeringmeyer, describe astronauts returning with one leg shorter than the other, which he attributed to magnetic field deficiency syndrome and treated with a north pole magnet in the shoe. Coming from a culture steeped in duality, Goiz wondered why nobody used the opposite pole. His first experiment, as Austin tells it, was on a gravely ill man who is reportedly still alive today."}, {"title": "What the legs are actually telling you", "body": "Austin explains that biomagnetism always uses magnets in pairs, red for north and black for south, held for a time based on your latitude, which he says lets the body restore pH and homeostasis. The scan begins at the feet, because in his practice a magnet placed over an imbalance makes one leg visibly shorten. Austin says roughly eighty percent of people walk around with a small discrepancy, which Goiz linked to a pH contraction in tiny muscle groups after trauma rather than a displaced hip. Chance describes a client with a six inch difference whose chiropractor, he says, could not explain the sudden correction after one biofield session."}, {"title": "Emotions, mirrors and the body as a yes or no machine", "body": "Austin now weighs his practice as half pathogenic and half emotional, and sometimes closer to ninety percent emotional. He describes tracing a family member's sudden symptom to seven emotions, muscle testing how many days it would take to clear, and says it cleared in four. Chance explains how he reads repressed anger as a load on the liver and colon, and recalls Eileen pointing out that he bruised his foot kicking his dog right after kicking himself over his career. Both describe learning a private signal, a click or a leg shift, that lets the body answer yes or no."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Austin Walters is a Biomagnetism researcher, teacher, and practitioner, a technique that uses magnets to balance the biofield, similar to using sound. We learn about stepping stones in his journey to his modality, with stepping stones like colloidal silver, pulsed electromagnetic field devices, pH and leg length discrepancy, and his ability to use his own body as a surrogate for clients during remote sessions.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, we talk about knowledge of cancer, based on his care for his late wife, internal fungal decomposition, caring for the biological terrain, muscle testing to talk to the body, the power of the name, sleeping with magnets, and much more.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Illness as the body's attempt to restore balance", "body": "Austin Walters argues that every process the body runs, even one that looks harmful, is an attempt to return to homeostasis. He offers osteoporosis as an example, suggesting the body may draw calcium from bone to buffer acidity rather than simply lacking calcium. He describes what biomagnetism calls the tumoral phenomenon, a category covering any abnormal tissue growth, and asks why the body is making it. His baking the cake image frames illness as many ingredients combining, including emotions, environment and pathogens, which he believes explains why two people with similar habits can have very different outcomes."}, {"title": "Terrain theory, germ theory, and a middle path", "body": "Chance Garton raises research suggesting bacteria act as cleanup crews that change form to suit their environment, and Austin Walters connects this to Antoine Béchamp and pleomorphism, contrasting it with the Louis Pasteur model he says medicine adopted. Austin lands between the two views, estimating that most illness comes down to terrain, meaning emotional state and what enters the body, while allowing that a pathogen placed where it does not belong can still cause trouble. He uses a urinary tract example to show how he sees magnets shifting pH so bacteria lose their foothold, and shares a developing theory about viruses."}, {"title": "Muscle testing as a conversation with the body", "body": "Austin Walters compares muscle testing to making a fist: nobody knows how they do it, yet the body simply responds. In a biomagnetism session the client lies clothed on a table while he gently jiggles the feet and watches for a leg length shift that he reads as a yes. He stresses removing practitioner error and staying neutral, calling himself a detective and facilitator rather than a healer. He describes working from roughly 350 magnet pairs plus an emotion sheet across sessions of about ninety minutes to two hours. Chance Garton likens different testing tools to different languages expressing one idea."}, {"title": "Intention as the deciding factor", "body": "Austin Walters believes intention is the make or break element of his therapy. Because many structures share one region of the neck, he directs each magnet toward a specific target, and he says more specific intention brings more specific results. Chance Garton describes opening his Biofield Tuning sessions by naming a higher intelligence as the force doing the work, with practitioners as its paintbrush. He explains how dowsing rods help him map a client's field quickly, and how his own ears popping and shifting pressure now tell him where to work and which tuning fork to choose."}, {"title": "Remote work, ritual, and teaching others", "body": "Austin Walters explains how he works remotely, testing on his own arms and placing magnet pairs on a flat anatomical figure while holding the client's name and location in mind. He links the power of a written name to Masaru Emoto's water experiments and says he now finds remote sessions just as effective and more focused. Chance Garton shares his own ritual of crystals, candles and sweeping the room before each session, though he prefers being live on the call. Both close by saying they would rather people learn these tools themselves, with Austin rejecting a mindset of scarcity among practitioners."}]
